findings.quote: It does not reach clean-label accuracy at this noise rate, and on breast cancer it recovers only 22\%\src{recovery_bc_n40} of the loss.
We show that the out-of-fold disagreement of a logistic regression with a training label is a precise and high-recall detector of flipped labels on two datasets under symmetric noise.
We show that it improves over logistic regression and over an untuned MLP on the same noisy labels, costs little on clean labels, and report where it falls short.
findings.fix: Add the scope: 'improves over logistic regression at 40% noise on both datasets and at 20% on digits (not significant on breast cancer at 20%), and over an untuned MLP at 20% and 40% noise'. The MLP is ahead on clean digits.

A linear model's disagreement on held-out folds is enough to find most flipped labels, and acting on it is cheap.
For a linear model under label noise, the out-of-fold filter is the baseline that more elaborate methods should report against.

findings.quote: It discards clean samples: a quarter to a third of the drop set is correctly labeled.
On breast cancer at 40\%\src{noise_max_pct} noise it recovers only 22.1\%\src{recovery_bc_n40} of the lost accuracy, and on both datasets it stays below clean-label accuracy at that rate.
A softer rule, such as a confidence threshold, reweighting instead of dropping, or a second filtering round, may close the gap.

The filter costs more to fit than logistic regression on digits (0.056\,s\src{fit_sec_digits_filter} against 0.012\,s\src{fit_sec_digits_logreg}), but less than the MLP (0.56\,s\src{fit_sec_digits_mlp}); this is one timing on one machine.
We study two small datasets, symmetric noise up to 40\%\src{noise_max_pct}, 5\src{n_seeds} seeds, one $K$ and one $C$, and one untuned MLP.
We make no claim about deep networks or large data.
